- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.40) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect downward — adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive pessimism.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., > +2.0% from prior peak), model often overshoots and fails to mean-revert — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% and add a slight downward slope.  
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (e.g., 0.0 to +0.30), model frequently underestimates upward momentum — increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% for next 3–5 days.  
- Model consistently underestimates true price in early 30-day horizon — add 0.8–1.2% to forecast for first 7–10 days if sentiment is stable or mildly bullish.  
- When sentiment turns positive after a prolonged negative streak, model delays reaction — forecast should begin rising 2–3 days earlier than true outcome.  
- If model forecast is below 60.0 and sentiment is negative, avoid sharp downward revisions — instead, assume slight upward bias due to market stabilization.  
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome exceeds model by >1.5% in 3 consecutive days, apply a “mean reversion” correction: reduce forecast by 0.3–0.7% per day until convergence.
